newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori hits new low in approval rating.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori hits new low in approval rating.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori hit a new low in his approval rating on Wednesday amid public outrage over a phone-tapping scandal and the annulment of an Israeli-born businessman's citizenship.
The survey by leading local pollster Apoyo put Fujimori's popularity at 23 percent -- his lowest in seven years of power and a fall of 11 percent in just nine days.
The poll, of around 400 Lima area residents, also showed that 53 percent believe the military controlled the real power in Peru. Only 38 percent said Fujimori held the reins.

Peru's security forces are widely accused of being behind the weekend revocation of local citizenship for the owner of the Frecuencia Latina T.V. channel, Baruch Ivcher, and a phone-tapping scandal revealed by the same station.

Frecuencia Latina had broken a string of stories alleging human rights abuses and corruption in the security forces, culminating in Sunday's airing of a report on phone-tapping by secret services just an hour before the move against Ivcher.

Fujimori, in an interview with Spanish news agency Efe, blamed his political problems on a "sophisticated, psycho-political campaign" by the opposition to present him as a dictator running a police state.

"The main proof that democracy exists in Peru is that there is a strong opposition, and I celebrate that there is, that (the opposition) is not in jail nor persecuted, nor exiled, nor prevented from doing regular and democratic politics," he said.

Fujimori avoided saying if he backed the revocation of Ivcher's nationality via a decree last Sunday signed by a police chief, but added he had given "precise instructions" to the judiciary to clarify the matter.

Regarding the phone-tapping, Fujimori noted he and his security adviser Vladimiro Montesinos had their conversations taped in 1992. "It is public knowledge that these devices (to tap phones) can be easily obtained in the market," he added.

In the Apoyo poll, Montesinos, considered Fujimori's right-hand man and his bridge with the military, received the approval of nine percent of respondents and disapproval of 79 percent. Armed forces chief Gen. Nicolas de Bari Hermoza won 15 percent approval and 67 percent disapproval. The survey gave no margin of error.
Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi, speaking to reporters late on Tuesday, pledged the government would "get to the bottom" of the phone allegations and punish those found responsible.
Frecuencia Latina had alleged 197 people, including journalists, politicians, diplomats, businessmen and artists, were the subject of phone-tapping.

That scandal, and the revocation of Ivcher's nationality on grounds of bureaucratic "irregularities," sparked a wave of media and public condemnation and has become a rallying point for Peru's rejuvenated opposition.

The timing could hardly be worse for Fujimori, who has slid steadily in popularity since his 70 percent showing after masterminding the spectacular end of a four-month hostage crisis in Lima on April 22.
